passages.text: Frankish communities expressed wealth and identity through dress and skilled metalwork. The map's Frankish Kingdom record covers only part of a longer history and should not imply that Frankish culture began in 600.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Women wore belted tunics with a wrap or cloak. Pendants hung from belts, and jewelry included earrings, necklaces and hairpins.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Small paired brooches were common in earlier centuries; large single disk brooches became fashionable in the 600s.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A mid-seventh-century disk brooch combines gold with garnet, colored glass and mother-of-pearl. Small fastening objects could display elaborate material contrasts.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768 and emperor in 800. Imperial culture grew from earlier Frankish traditions of patronage and fine metalwork.

passages.text: Funan, known from the reports of Chinese envoys in the third century, was the first of Southeast Asia's Indian-influenced states, in the Mekong delta. Its port at Oc Eo linked the trade of Rome, India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Oc Eo's canals and warehouses handled goods between the Gulf of Thailand and the Mekong; coins of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius were found there.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Indian beads and seals, Chinese bronze mirrors and local tin amulets came out of the excavations of the 1940s.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit inscriptions and images of Vishnu and Shiva show Indian religion at court, with Buddhism beside it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, who visited about 245, described walled towns, taxes paid in gold and a written script.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A network of canals, one of them nearly 90 kilometers long, drained and linked the delta towns.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Funan set the pattern of the Indianized kingdom that Chenla, the Chams and the Khmer followed.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Oc Eo is among the earliest excavated urban sites in mainland Southeast Asia.
In the sixth century the inland Khmer state the Chinese called Chenla absorbed Funan; by about 550 its kings ruled the delta.

passages.text: In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Genoa developed the Strade Nuove as a coordinated district of streets and aristocratic palaces above the older city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The palaces adapted to steep and confined sites with open staircases, courtyards and garden-facing loggias. Frescoes and stucco decorated their interiors.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Senate established the Rolli list of private palaces used to lodge distinguished official visitors. Hosting state guests became an obligation attached to selected elite homes.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Rolli system sorted residences into categories corresponding to different ranks of guest. Hospitality made social hierarchy part of the organization of official visits.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Architectural treatises spread knowledge of Genoa's new streets and palaces beyond the city in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

passages.text: Goguryeo was the largest and most martial of Korea's Three Kingdoms, holding the north of the peninsula and much of Manchuria from its mountain fortresses. Its painted tombs are the fullest picture of life in early Korea, and its art reached Japan through Baekje and its own monks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Tomb murals show hunts, processions, wrestlers, dancers, the sun crow and the moon toad, and the four directional animals, painted with a sense of movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze crown ornaments, earrings and belt fittings show skilled metalwork.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist sculpture and temple building grew after the religion arrived in 372; the gilt-bronze Buddha of 539 from Yeonga is the oldest dated Korean Buddhist image.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mountain fortresses of fitted stone, built to the ridgelines, guarded the valleys and river crossings.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron lamellar armor for horse and rider equipped heavy cavalry, as the tomb paintings show.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Sundo arrived from Former Qin with images and sutras, and the court adopted Buddhism; a Confucian academy, the Taehak, was founded the same year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native shamanic and ancestral rites continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs in North Korea and the capitals and tombs of the kingdom in China were both listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the tenth-century dynasty that took its name from Goguryeo.

After decades of war with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when Pyongyang was taken in 668. Tang set up a protectorate over the north; Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river and pushed the Tang armies out by 676.

passages.text: The Göktürk Khaganate was the first empire to bear the name Türk. Founded by Bumin in 552, it stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea, split into eastern and western halves in 583, submitted to Tang in 630 and 657, and rose again as the Second Khaganate in 682. Its stone inscriptions are the oldest Turkic writing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The stelae of Kül Tegin (732) and Bilge Qaghan (735) in the Orkhon valley carry the oldest long texts in the Old Turkic script, the first Turkic writing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Tengri, the sky, gave the khagan his mandate; shamans and the sacred Ötüken forest stood at the center of belief.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Taspar Qaghan patronized Buddhism and had sutras translated into Turkic, though Tengri worship remained the rule.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The khaganate held the Silk Road from China to Persia, with Sogdian merchants as its traders and scribes.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Sogdian Maniakh, an envoy of the khagan, reached Constantinople to open a silk route around Sasanian Persia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Türk first appears in history with this empire.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Orkhon inscriptions remain the chief source for early Turkic language and history.
An alliance of Uyghur, Basmyl and Karluk tribes overthrew the khaganate; the Uyghur Khaganate rose in its place in 744.

passages.text: Goryeo, founded by Wang Geon in 918, ruled a united Korea from 936 and gave the country its name. Its Buddhist court produced jade-green celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana and the first books printed from metal type.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: A ritual text, the Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun, was printed from metal movable type by the record of the time, more than two centuries before Gutenberg; the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist canon in Chinese script, was carved on more than 81,000 wooden blocks between 1236 and 1251 as a prayer for deliverance from the Mongols.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Celadon with a jade-green glaze and inlaid black and white designs reached its height in the twelfth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist paintings on silk, gilt-bronze sculpture and sutras written in gold and silver on indigo paper.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Tripitaka blocks have been kept at Haeinsa temple since 1398 and can still be printed from after nearly 800 years.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was the state faith, with temples, festivals and monks who held rank at court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Chinese classics and composition began under King Gwangjong, with separate examinations for monks.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, carried west by merchants and travelers.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Haeinsa's depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana were listed by UNESCO; the celadons are national treasures.
General Yi Seong-gye, who had turned his army back from a campaign against Ming in 1388, deposed the last Goryeo king and took the throne in 1392 as the founder of Joseon.

Food, farming and differences within society

passages.text: Great Moravia was a ninth-century political formation ruled by the Mojmirid dynasty. Mikulcice preserves evidence of its centres, including bridges, churches, workshops and food remains. Slavic literary work accompanied religious and diplomatic change. Its political collapse in the early tenth century did not erase the population or every settlement; the map's 900-1000 interval is not its historical lifetime.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: Mikulcice occupied raised ground within the Morava floodplain. Its ninth-century defences combined timber and earth with a stone-facing wall. Waterways shaped both access and protection, making engineering part of everyday movement through the settlement.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: Archaeologists found wooden bridge remains in former river channels around Mikulcice. These crossings connected the fortified core with surrounding occupied areas, giving physical evidence of routes that no longer follow today's river course.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: The Czech archaeological atlas records a Great Moravian dugout canoe lifted at Mikulcice in 1967. The surviving vessel complements the bridge evidence for movement on and across water; 1967 dates its recovery, not its construction.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: The acropolis contained a basilica and a building interpreted as a palace, while residential quarters extended into the outer bailey and beyond. Churchyards and burials help reconstruct institutions, but the entire population did not live inside the elite core.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: Mikulcice's plant remains include millet, wheat, rye, barley and oats. Millet dominates seed counts, but the archaeobotanical study shows that rankings change when weight and food value are considered. Many small seeds do not automatically mean most calories.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: Grape pips survived at Mikulcice as charred, mineralised and waterlogged remains. Their shapes raise questions about wild grapes and older cultivated varieties. Finding pips establishes grape use more securely than a particular vineyard, wine recipe or grape variety.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: A study of adults buried by Mikulcice's Church VI compared tooth and bone chemistry from the same people. The researchers interpreted the differences as more millet and less animal protein in childhood than adulthood, recovering changes within individual lives.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: The same study linked inferred social position with dietary differences, including greater animal-protein consumption among the elite. These findings concern the sampled cemetery population, rather than proving a uniform diet across all of Great Moravia.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: Great Moravian pottery includes both specialist workshop products and simpler domestic manufacture. The archaeological institute stresses that techniques changed at different speeds and served different customers, rather than replacing all older practices at once.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: A ninth-century silver chain earring from Mikulcice illustrates fine metalworking. Other elite jewellery used filigree and granulation alongside simpler ornaments. Finished objects show technical skill, but do not by themselves establish whether knowledge travelled with visiting artisans or returning apprentices.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: The institute also illustrates a ninth-century antler playing piece from Mikulcice decorated with a bowman. This small object adds leisure and imagery to a record often dominated by churches, weapons and prestigious graves.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: Constantine, later called Cyril, developed Glagolitic letters for Slavic religious writing. With Methodius, he helped build a literary and teaching tradition tied to Moravia's church diplomacy. Their mission entered a region where Christian institutions already existed.

The Mojmirid political structure collapsed in the early tenth century under Magyar pressure and internal strain. This ended a state, not its entire society. Reduced occupation at Mikulcice and the later reuse of Moravian identity make total depopulation an unsuitable description; the exact sequence remains debated.

passages.text: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders fitted local granite slabs together without mortar. Successive courses stepped inward, giving the curving walls a stabilizing inward slope.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Eight surviving soapstone bird sculptures combine human and bird features. Their precise meaning remains uncertain; an association with royal authority is one interpretation.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Stone walls stood beside homes made from daga, a building material of earth, with thatched roofs. Painted surfaces and enclosed courtyards formed parts of the lived settlement.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavations recovered imported glass beads, ceramics from China and Persia, and coins from Kilwa. These objects place the inland settlement within long-distance exchange networks; they do not, by themselves, identify every trader or route.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Six soapstone birds came from the Hill Complex's Eastern Enclosure. Their setting supports interpretations involving ritual or royal authority, but their original arrangement and precise meaning remain uncertain.

Great Zimbabwe did not simply empty in 1450. A study combining radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and imported objects places occupation at least into the sixteenth century and probably the seventeenth, after its main building peak in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The chronology does not identify a single conquest or establish one cause for the loss of political prominence. The site remains a place of spiritual practice for contemporary communities; the decline of a capital did not mean the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Greek city-states formed a varied political and cultural world. These examples focus on Athens and Classical sculpture; Athenian institutions should not be assumed to describe every Greek community.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Athenian potters controlled the air admitted to a kiln in successive firing stages to produce contrasting black and red surfaces.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red-figure vase painting developed around 530 BCE. Brush-drawn details gave painters greater freedom to show anatomy, fabric and movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polykleitos developed a system of bodily proportions. Many renowned Greek bronze compositions are known through later marble copies and written descriptions.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The marble Parthenon belonged to the building program associated with Perikles and the worship of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: In Classical Athens, adult male citizens participated in the assembly. This was a particular civic institution, not political participation for every resident.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Different vessel shapes served storage, water carrying, drinking and ritual. Pottery images complement written evidence about Athenian life.

passages.text: Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, weirs and dams. These connected structures trapped, held and harvested kooyang, the short-finned eel.

passages.title: Science and environment
passages.text: Aquaculture depended on knowledge of seasonal eel movement, water flow and wetland ecology. Water management and food production were linked practices.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites alongside eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. Settlement and food processing belong in the same landscape.

passages.title: Arts and knowledge
passages.text: Storytelling, dance and basket weaving transmit knowledge across generations. Fibre baskets also belong to the practical technology of eel harvesting.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A cultural weir restored traditional flows into Tae Rak after earlier drainage. Gunditjmara customary responsibilities and cultural connections continue today.

passages.text: The Guptas ruled a large part of northern India during a period of influential mathematics, Sanskrit learning and religious art. Surviving temples, inscriptions and metalwork reveal the skills of craftspeople and the ambitions of patrons. These achievements belonged to a wider South Asian world: a work described as Gupta-period was not necessarily commissioned by a Gupta emperor.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura, usually associated with Pataliputra. It brings together mathematical rules and astronomical calculation, including a sine table and an approximation of pi equal to 3.1416.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: His method called kuttaka reduces problems about whole-number solutions to smaller steps. Such mathematics helped address astronomical questions about recurring planetary periods.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata used an alphabetic system to express numbers. Historians infer familiarity with place value, but that is different from a securely dated claim that he or the Gupta court invented the written zero.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: The iron pillar now at Delhi's Qutb complex is associated with Chandragupta II. Its survival offers material evidence of skilled ironworking; its present location alone does not identify its original setting.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: Analysis of the pillar's rust identified a protective layer containing iron phosphate. The study connects its unusual corrosion resistance to phosphorus in the iron and repeated wetting and drying, rather than to iron that never rusts.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: A sandstone seated Buddha from Uttar Pradesh, now at the Metropolitan Museum, is dated to the first quarter of the fifth century. It is a specific surviving example of Gupta-period sculpture; the collection record does not establish an excavated findspot.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: At Bhitargaon, builders used brick for a temple with a tall spire and terracotta panels of deities. India's heritage nomination dates it to the middle of the fifth century on stylistic grounds and leaves its dedication to Vishnu or Shiva unresolved.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: The early sixth-century temple at Deogarh preserves elaborate stone carving and part of its tower. Alongside Bhitargaon, it shows that builders developed temple forms in different materials, rather than following a single construction technique.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: Ajanta's later Buddhist caves belong to the same broad cultural period, but their patrons were Vakataka rulers and their feudatories. Their paintings should not be presented as a commission of the Gupta imperial court.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The Mandsaur silk-weavers' inscription describes craftspeople moving from Lata to Dashapura with children and relatives. It preserves a community's account of migration and skilled work, although its praise of the city is commemorative poetry, not a household survey.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The guild commemorated repairs to a Sun temple it had financed from its craft earnings. The inscription recalls the original foundation in 437 to 438 CE, showing artisans pooling resources for worship and maintenance across generations.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: Provincial and district officials governed alongside village institutions. Inscriptions also record trade guilds, while control of western ports connected the empire with overseas commerce. These institutions help explain the world beyond the royal court.

passages.title: Traditions beyond the dynasty
passages.text: Gupta-period sculptors developed Buddha images that influenced later Buddhist art across Asia. An artistic tradition could travel beyond the empire and outlast its rulers; the political endpoint of a dynasty is not the end of its cultural influence.

Gupta imperial rule broke apart through regional independence and repeated invasions, rather than one conquest by a single successor. Maitraka and Maukhari rulers were among the powers that emerged. Around 550 marks the conventional end of the imperial dynasty; communities and artistic traditions continued under changing governments.

passages.text: Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Northern and southern suburbs developed in the thirteenth century around the older central medina. Tunis was an expanding urban settlement, not only a palace city.

passages.title: Arts and exchange
passages.text: Tunis connected the Maghreb, southern Europe and lands to the east. These links encouraged exchanges in architecture and the arts.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Souqs, residential quarters and gates formed an interconnected townscape. Their survival helps historians study urban organization alongside individual monuments.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Mosques and madrasas belonged to the city's institutional landscape. Surviving examples span both the Hafsid era and later periods.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Subsequent rulers added new palaces, residences and religious buildings. The medina records continuity and change across political transitions.

passages.text: The Han ruled China for four centuries, with a brief interruption, and set the pattern that later dynasties followed: an emperor advised by scholar-officials trained in the Confucian classics, a census-taking bureaucracy, and a capital laid out on a grid. Paper, the seismoscope and the first great history of China were made under the Han, and the Silk Road opened during their reign. The Chinese still call their majority people the Han.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Cai Lun presents the court with paper made from bark, hemp and rags. Paper travels west along the Silk Road and reaches Europe a thousand years later.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope: a bronze vessel that dropped a ball into one of eight dragon mouths to show the direction of a distant earthquake.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The wheelbarrow, the crank handle and the stern-mounted rudder are all first attested in Han China.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Taichu calendar reform sets the civil year, with its intercalary months, on the footing that Chinese calendars follow in principle to this day.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: systems of linear equations solved by a method equivalent to Gaussian elimination, rules for negative numbers, and an approximation of pi.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zhang Heng's water-driven armillary sphere turns with the heavens, and he catalogues about 2,500 stars.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Xu Shen's Shuowen Jiezi, the first dictionary to analyse Chinese characters by their components, is presented to the throne.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Du Shi harnesses a water wheel to the bellows of a blast furnace. Cast iron becomes cheap enough for ploughshares and hoes.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brine wells drilled hundreds of meters deep with bamboo derricks in Sichuan, and natural gas piped through bamboo to boil the brine for salt.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Silk woven on multi-shaft treadle looms. Han silks have been found in Roman-era graves at Palmyra in Syria.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The tombs at Mawangdui are sealed, preserving silk paintings, a silk map, and the earliest complete copies of the Daodejing.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, 130 chapters covering two thousand years and the model for every later Chinese dynastic history.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The fu rhapsodies of Sima Xiangru, the folk songs collected by the Music Bureau, and lacquerware from Sichuan workshops exported across Asia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Wu makes the Confucian classics the basis of official learning; the Imperial Academy follows in 124 BCE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The White Horse Temple at Luoyang, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, marks the arrival of Buddhism along the Silk Road.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Chong's Lunheng argues that thunder is not the anger of heaven and that the dead have no consciousness.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhang Daoling founds the Way of the Celestial Masters in Sichuan, the first organized Daoist religion.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zhang Qian sets out for the west. His reports of Ferghana horses, Parthia and India open what is now called the Silk Road.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Protectorate of the Western Regions is set up in the Tarim Basin, securing the route to Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: An embassy claiming to come from the Roman emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court by sea, according to the Book of Later Han.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The census counts 57,671,400 people, most of them farming households of about five on small plots of millet, wheat and rice, taxed in grain, cloth and labour.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an, the Western Han capital, sits inside about 25 km of walls with nine markets, and is one of the two largest cities in the world alongside Rome.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Games of liubo and cuju kickball, and the clay tomb figures of dancers, farmyards and watchtowers that show the Han world in miniature.

Weakened by court factions and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184, the dynasty ended when Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian in 220. China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.

passages.text: The Heian period was the high age of the Japanese court. With the Fujiwara regents running politics from Heian-kyo, the aristocracy turned to poetry, calligraphy and romance, and its women wrote the first great works of Japanese prose.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sei Shonagon finished The Pillow Book, her lists and observations of court life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The kana syllabaries took shape, so that Japanese could be written without Chinese.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Phoenix Hall of Byodoin at Uji was built for the Fujiwara, with its Amida by the sculptor Jocho.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Saicho founded Tendai on Mount Hiei and Kukai brought Shingon from China, the esoteric schools of the court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Genshin's Essentials of Rebirth spread devotion to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The sensibility of mono no aware, the pathos of passing things, ran through court writing.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Aristocratic life turned on poetry contests, music, calligraphy, incense and love affairs conducted by letter.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court women, writing in kana, produced the diaries and tales that define the age.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tale of Genji remains at the center of Japanese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The kana syllabaries are still the core of Japanese writing.
The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in the Genpei War, ending at Dan-no-ura in 1185; Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled from Kamakura and was named shogun in 1192.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing confederacy of nations. The Onondaga Nation's own accounts describe government, food, ceremonies and wampum as living practices connecting community responsibilities with historical memory.

passages.title: Government
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the Hoyane who represent their clans in council. They can remove a leader who fails to represent the clan, after warnings.

passages.title: Technology and memory
passages.text: Wampum makers cut, round, sand and drill shell beads. Woven strings and belts support the remembrance of agreements and their histories.

passages.title: Diplomacy
passages.text: Wampum strings can carry invitations to council meetings. They also identify leadership titles and give weight to a speaker's words.

passages.title: Food and daily life
passages.text: Corn, beans and squash are the Three Sisters. Onondaga food traditions also include fishing, hunting, gathering and sharing food within the community.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Thanksgiving Address opens gatherings by acknowledging people, the natural world and their interdependence. Speakers express it in their own words.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Clan Mothers help sustain ceremonies and teach younger generations. These are present-day responsibilities, not customs of a vanished society.

sectionTitles: Art and institutions across political change

passages.text: The medieval Kingdom of Hungary connected monasteries, towns, farms and royal courts across a territory larger than modern Hungary. Surviving textiles, vessels, tiles and books reveal imported skills alongside local production. Ottoman expansion and rival claims to the crown divided political authority in the sixteenth century, while communities and institutions continued under different governments.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996, before the kingdom conventionally dated from 1000. Its churches were rebuilt repeatedly. The church begun in 1224 contains earlier remains, making the complex evidence of successive communities rather than one untouched medieval building.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Pannonhalma's red-marble Porta Speciosa leads into a cloister built in 1486. Later alterations changed doors and windows. Traces of an earlier cloister and refectory entrance show how prayer, movement and communal meals shaped the monastery's built environment.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A centaur-shaped bronze hand-washing vessel in the Hungarian National Museum was made at Hildesheim in the 1220s. Its arrival in Hungary may reflect court connections. The object demonstrates imported metalworking and elite washing practices, not a Hungarian invention of the form.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: The gilded-silver vessel from Beszterec, dated to the later eleventh century, carries a Greek inscription and animal ornament. Its partly reconstructed supports matter when reading its present appearance. Byzantine manufacture and religious use connected the kingdom with another artistic world.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Stephen and Gisela donated the textile now called the Coronation Mantle to the Szekesfehervar basilica in 1031. It began as a priestly vestment and later entered coronation ritual. A surviving object could acquire new political meaning long after its first use.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Late-fifteenth-century tiles from the Bothar workshop at Besztercebanya, now Banska Bystrica, include glazed images of saints. Unfinished and spoiled pieces survived as well. They reveal production behind the decorated stoves that changed domestic heating, rather than only finished luxury objects.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: A leather spectacle frame dated before 1470 was found behind an altar panel at Liptoszentandras, now Liptovsky Ondrej. It is direct evidence of an aid to sight. Its hiding place does not identify its wearer or establish how many people owned spectacles.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Fifteenth-century printed missals left blank spaces for initials and pictures to be painted by hand. Printing therefore worked alongside skilled manual decoration. The finished pages preserve cooperation between old and new methods of making books.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Matthias's Corvina library commissioned decorated manuscripts at Buda as well as obtaining Italian books. Study of the codex containing Pietro Ranzano's history of Hungary reassigned its production from Naples to Buda, showing why an Italian-looking style does not prove an Italian workshop.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: The library's surviving bindings and illumination help reconstruct an organised late-fifteenth-century workshop. High-ranking church patrons also ordered its books. These manuscripts record collaborative specialist labour and patronage, as well as the writings preserved on their pages.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The Nyirbator choir stalls name their Bathory patrons and the year 1511; another panel carries the maker's mark F. Marone. Inlaid cupboards display books and kitchen utensils. The furniture brings images of familiar possessions into an elaborate setting for worship.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The division of Hungary left several settings for skilled work. The museum documents mining and guild production in Royal Hungary, while Hutterite communities moving there and later to Transylvania practised tin-glazed pottery. Political boundaries did not halt the movement of craftspeople.

The defeat of 1526 and Ottoman occupation of Buda in 1541 unfolded in stages. Rival kingship, Ottoman conquest and the emergence of Transylvania divided the medieval kingdom. Habsburg rulers retained the Hungarian crown in Royal Hungary; neither 1492, the imported map endpoint, nor one battle marks the disappearance of Hungarian society.

passages.text: Awfāt, usually called Ifat, was a Muslim sultanate on the Ethiopian highland escarpment. Excavations distinguish its capital and royal cemetery from other towns, including Nora.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: Nora’s houses used stone and earth mortar, with niches in their walls. Pottery lay on earthen floors. Streets and open spaces connected the buildings.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: Unglazed pottery, imported beads and cowries survived at Nora. Iron rods may relate to currency described in medieval texts, but that identification remains a hypothesis.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: The 2008 excavations examined houses and two of Nora’s five mosques. The resulting volume studies pottery, glass, metal and animal remains together. A town’s history comes from ordinary discarded material as well as its largest buildings.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: Nora had a Great Mosque and four smaller neighbourhood mosques. Their distribution places religious buildings among residential areas. The large congregational building was only one part of the town’s religious landscape.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: The Great Mosque changed over time. Earlier stone columns were made from single pieces; a later phase used assembled column elements. Rebuilding altered how the roof was supported.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: In the small mosque labelled M2, one central column supported the prayer room. A courtyard lay to the south, while the prayer niche marked its northern side.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: A worked stone object near M2 was interpreted as a basin for ritual washing. The interpretation connects an object with preparation for prayer, although its precise use is not directly recorded.

passages.title: Inscriptions and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Walasma tomb inscriptions preserve names, religious invocations and dates in the 1360s and 1370s. They provide evidence for the dynasty independent of later narrative histories.

passages.title: Inscriptions and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Nora’s occupation is dated broadly from the late thirteenth century to the first third of the sixteenth. That range describes a settlement, not a single ruler’s reign or an exact date when all its inhabitants left.

Awfāt probably lost its capital status after 1376. Later warfare brought Christian royal control over Ifat, while the Walasma dynasty continued elsewhere. Disagreements about rulers’ dates and continuing towns make a single universal “fall” date misleading.

passages.text: Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Road builders used bridges, stairs, paving and drainage suited to different terrain. The network linked centers of production, government and worship.

passages.title: Food and farming
passages.text: Communities built and maintained terraces that created level planting areas while resisting erosion. Water conduits also protected roads from damaging runoff.

passages.title: Water engineering
passages.text: Stone channels and storage facilities managed rainfall and snowmelt for resources shared among families.

passages.title: Storage
passages.text: Colcas were storehouses whose siting and construction kept supplies cool and dry. Their contents included potatoes, maize, quinoa, clothing and tools.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The road system moved goods including textiles, feathers, food and shell. It incorporated earlier routes and knowledge from Andean communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Andean languages and traditions continued under Spanish rule. Weavers combined established textile techniques and designs with new imagery.
Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532 and had him killed in 1533. Spanish conquest dismantled imperial government, while Andean peoples continued and adapted their traditions.

passages.text: The Jin dynasty briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but internal weakness and uprisings by the peoples of the north led to the loss of the north in 316. The Eastern Jin survived in the south as a center of Chinese culture.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion, the most admired piece of Chinese calligraphy, at a spring gathering of poets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting begins to emerge as an independent art form; Gu Kaizhi paints the Admonitions scroll.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Huiyuan founds a Buddhist community on Mount Lu; translation projects and monasteries multiply.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Faxian sets out for India to collect Buddhist texts, and returns by sea fifteen years later.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, of the Wei to Jin transition, exemplify literati withdrawal and philosophical debate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Eastern Jin preserved Chinese high culture in the south while the north underwent ethnic mixing.
The last Eastern Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, a powerful general who founded the Liu Song dynasty.

passages.text: Joseon ruled Korea for more than five centuries under a Neo-Confucian order. King Sejong's court gave the country its alphabet, Hangul, and a run of scientific instruments; the dynasty survived Japanese and Manchu invasions and lasted, as the Korean Empire after 1897, until Japan annexed it in 1910.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: King Sejong created Hangul, published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, so that ordinary people could read and write.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The cheugugi rain gauge, a standard cylinder read against a ruler, was set up across the provinces, nearly two centuries before the first European rain gauge of 1639.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Jang Yeong-sil's self-striking water clock, the Jagyeongnu, and armillary spheres and sundials for the royal observatory.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Chiljeongsan calendar reform computed the motions of the sun, moon and planets for Seoul's own meridian.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Heo Jun's Donguibogam, a medical encyclopedia, was published.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: White porcelain, plain or painted in cobalt blue, became the ware of the scholar's table.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, a daily record of every reign from 1392 to 1863, among the longest continuous histories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became state orthodoxy; Buddhism lost its land and court standing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Confucian classics selected officials, and the yangban scholar class ran the state.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and cannon fleets cut the Japanese supply lines during the invasions of 1592 to 1598.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Gunpowder weapons, from hwacha rocket carts to ship-borne cannon, were made at state arsenals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Hangul is the writing system of both Koreas today.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucian family and social values shaped Korean life for centuries.
Joseon was proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 under the same royal house. Japan made it a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.

passages.text: The Kamakura period brought Japan's first warrior government. The shogunate at Kamakura ruled beside the old court in Kyoto, the samurai became the ruling class, and new Buddhist schools, Zen among them, reached both warriors and common people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China, and Dogen founded Soto Zen in 1227; meditation and discipline appealed to the warriors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Honen's Pure Land school, then Shinran's True Pure Land and Nichiren's Lotus school of 1253, offered salvation to ordinary people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Warrior ideals of loyalty and service took shape, later codified as bushido.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Unkei and the Kei school carved lifelike portraits of monks and guardian figures with inlaid crystal eyes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze Amida more than 11 meters high, was cast.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Emaki handscrolls told war tales and temple legends; ink painting arrived with the Zen monks.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Samurai held land as vassals of the shogun and lived by the sword and the bow.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The court in Kyoto kept its ceremonies and titles while Kamakura held the armies and the law.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Mongol invasion fleets were repelled in 1274 and 1281, the second wrecked by a typhoon later called the kamikaze.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Shoguns governed Japan for nearly 700 years, until 1868.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zen shaped Japanese gardens, tea, ink painting and the martial arts.
Forces loyal to Emperor Go-Daigo took Kamakura in 1333. Ashikaga Takauji turned on the emperor and set up a new shogunate in Kyoto in 1336, the start of the Muromachi period.

passages.text: Kanem, east of Lake Chad, was the earlier heartland of Sayfawa power. Its beginnings remain uncertain; excavated settlements illuminate elite buildings and working materials.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: At Tié Kalaté S2, discarded bricks lie in a depression where clay was extracted and fired. Nearby residences stood on dunes.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: Tié’s substantial enclosure is a candidate for Njimi, the royal capital. The identification remains argued rather than confirmed by a naming inscription.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: A study of excavated iron nails distinguishes four main forms used in twelfth- to fourteenth-century Kanem. These ordinary fasteners preserve metalworking choices that monumental buildings alone cannot show. Their precise use must be established from archaeological context.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: At Tié, glass dominates the recovered beads, alongside smaller numbers made from ostrich eggshell, metal and stone. Bone pendants and cowries also served as ornaments. This assemblage describes personal adornment at the excavated site, not everyone’s dress.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Many glass beads are tiny cylinders or rounded forms. Makers cut drawn glass and often reheated it to soften sharp edges. Red-brown and yellow shades were common in the recovered collection.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Chemical analysis links a few beads with the glass industry around Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria. Much of the remaining glass has affinities farther east. The results support African exchange connections, while the exact routes and intermediaries remain uncertain.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: The Arabic Diwan preserves a royal succession record. Historians compare its chronology with other texts and archaeological dates.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Saharan exchange included enslaved people, horses and cloth. The court’s connections rested partly on coercion as well as commerce.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Cairo was an important meeting point for pilgrims from Kanem and later Borno travelling toward Mecca. Dewière’s study treats pilgrimage as religious practice that also carried people, goods and ideas between African regions.
In the late fourteenth century, the Sayfawa court left Kanem for Borno under pressure from Bulala rivals. Kanem continued under other rulers while the dynasty rebuilt its power west of the lake.

passages.text: Borno developed west of Lake Chad as a centre of Sayfawa government and scholarship. Its history includes scholarly communities, farming settlements and changing dynasties, as well as royal capitals.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: At Garumele, a settlement associated with Borno’s history, excavators found abundant fish remains together with sheep, goat and cattle bones. Oral traditions connect it with royalty, but its precise occupation dates and capital status remain debated.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: The range and quantity of fish at Garumele suggest specialist fishing. Researchers propose that some fish arrived already processed, while herders supplied livestock. These are interpretations of bone distributions, not proof of a known market organisation or preservation recipe.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Borno depended on agriculture. Many people combined farming with seasonal crafts or trade. Kyari Mohammed stresses the importance of regional commerce alongside Saharan routes, challenging a picture of an economy sustained only by distant caravans.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Some scholarly villages combined study with farming and enjoyed royal exemptions. Students advanced from Quran memorisation to Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu translation and interpretation. Education rested on organised communities as well as individual teachers.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: The Konduga Quran survives as loose leaves kept in a leather folder and satchel. Italian watermarks identify imported paper. Different hands added Arabic commentary and Old Kanembu glosses around the main text, preserving several readers’ work.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: A later copy of the Konduga manuscript’s final page preserved its annotations as well as its Quranic text. The copy used a different page layout. This unusual duplication protected a record of teaching, not only the main scriptural passage.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Owners patched the Konduga Quran with paper strips and stitches after moisture damaged its lower margins. Repeated repairs show care across generations. A surviving manuscript can record maintenance and reuse alongside the original scribe’s achievement.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Extensive written annotations became less common during nineteenth-century upheaval, but handwritten Qurans and oral translation continued. Bondarev proposes links with political and educational changes; he does not establish one decree that ended the practice.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Rabih’s administration demanded produce and other revenues through local authorities under military supervision. Mohammed’s research describes confiscation and punishment as tools of rule. These burdens make the occupation a history of households and livelihoods as well as battles.

Rabih conquered Borno in 1893. French forces and African allies defeated him in 1900; colonial partition followed. Royal institutions and regional communities continued under altered authority, while the independent state’s political order ended through successive conquests rather than a single timeless “fall.”

passages.text: Early medieval Kent joined royal households, farming communities, monasteries and overseas connections. Excavations at Lyminge preserve traces of feasting, games, textile work and changing diets; surviving manuscripts transmit Kentish laws. Royal independence ended through changing overlordship and West Saxon incorporation, while Canterbury's religious and educational institutions continued.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.

sectionTitles: Arts, education and the royal court

passages.text: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.

passages.text: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Kuba makers wove raffia palm fibers into cloth. Women joined, dyed and embellished panels with embroidery and applique.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cutting embroidered raffia threads created a dense pile surface. Some panels were displayed as prestige objects and used as currency rather than worn.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Multiple cloth panels formed wrappers whose gathered edges moved with the wearer. Dress combined bodily movement with elaborate surface design.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Ndop sculptures memorialized rulers through idealized seated figures and identifying symbols. A strategy board identifies Shyaam aMbul aNgoong.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Kuba chronologies preserve references to a solar eclipse and Halley's comet, giving historians points for comparison with independently dated celestial events.

passages.text: Gunaikurnai people maintain Country, kinship and cultural knowledge across Gippsland. Stoneworking traces at the Knob and exceptionally preserved wood at Cloggs Cave connect material evidence with knowledge held by communities. Their history includes colonial displacement, the survival of family connections and continuing care for land and waters.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: Gunaikurnai brings together the recorded names Gunnai and Kurnai in a form agreed by the community. Different spellings in older records often reflect how outsiders transcribed speech; they should not automatically be treated as different peoples.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: The Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation recognizes five major clans across Gippsland. Clan connections place responsibilities in particular landscapes, while families share wider relationships. A single outline on a map cannot capture all those connections.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: At the Knob on Brayakaulung Country, deep grooves in sandstone beneath the bluff record repeated sharpening of stone axe heads. Stone scatters, camps and scarred trees also survive, making this a landscape of skilled work as well as a gathering place.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Research published in 2024 described small fireplaces at Cloggs Cave near Buchan containing trimmed Casuarina sticks and fatty residues. Dating places these features about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago. The preserved wood provides unusually direct evidence of how people prepared and used plant materials.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Working with Gunaikurnai Elders, the Cloggs Cave researchers compared those finds with nineteenth-century descriptions of ritual specialists using treated sticks. They interpret a long transmission of ritual knowledge. The excavated objects and residues are observations; the connection across millennia is the study's argued interpretation.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Dooyeedang, the Avon River, linked high country with the Gippsland Lakes. Gunaikurnai accounts describe travel along it and foods including eels and fish. Moving through this river landscape connected meals and material resources with visits, exchange and relationships.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: The Knob hosted meetings where clans feasted, exchanged goods, shared news and held ceremonies. Such gatherings joined practical provisioning with social and cultural obligations; the place mattered for much more than a single activity.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Cultural fire is guided by knowledge of the season, the place and the purpose of a burn. Gunaikurnai accounts connect fire with land health, ceremony and communication. Renewing this practice draws on Elders' knowledge rather than treating every fire as an identical operation.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: During the mission era, people continued to meet at the Knob, sometimes secretly, to maintain family ties despite enforced separation. In 2010 the same place hosted the native title determination ceremony, linking legal recognition with a much older community history.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: Established in 2007, GLaWAC provides a community institution for representing Gunaikurnai people and caring for Country. Its public cultural protocols recognize that knowledge belongs to people and families and that perspectives within the community can differ.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: The Cultural Hub at Forestec supports community programs and cultural learning. Stories and songlines connect knowledge with ancestors and places; teaching involves relationships and responsibilities as well as information that can be written down.

Gunaikurnai communities continue. Colonial displacement and mission control disrupted families and access to Country, but neither ended the people or their knowledge. Native title recognition, cultural learning and care for Country are later chapters of that continuing history.

passages.text: Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron-working remains and ceramic production areas at Meroe document skilled manufacture. They establish local production, not a claim that Kush invented iron smelting.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Reservoirs helped support settlements away from the Nile. Their remains are evidence for both engineering and the environmental conditions in which people lived.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Steep-sided pyramids, decorated funerary chapels and painted burial chambers gave Kushite royal commemoration a distinctive appearance.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Architecture at Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat combined Kushite forms with elements associated with Egypt, Greece and Rome.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Gebel Barkal was a sacred landscape. Temples at its foot connected royal authority with the worship of Amun.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Meroitic political order ended in late antiquity, but burial traditions continued afterward. A kingdom's disappearance should not be read as the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Kushans, a Yuezhi clan from Bactria, built an empire from the Oxus to the Ganges in the first three centuries CE. They struck gold coins, stood at the crossing of the Silk Road, and under Kanishka became the great patrons of Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gandharan sculptors, drawing on Greek and Roman models, made some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, at the same time as the workshops of Mathura.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stupas and monasteries rose at Taxila, Peshawar and Hadda; Chinese pilgrims reported Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar as the tallest building they had seen.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire held the passes between the Silk Road, the Indus ports and the Ganges plain, and traded with Rome by sea and with Han China by land.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold coins on the Roman weight standard, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist gods, circulated from Central Asia to the Ganges.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kanishka's reign, beginning about 127 CE, is remembered in Buddhist tradition for a council in Kashmir that fixed the canon of the Sarvastivada school.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities all appear on Kushan coins, and Bactrian, written in Greek letters, was the language of the state.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Gandharan Buddhist art traveled along the Silk Road to Central Asia and China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Kushan patronage helped carry Buddhism to Central Asia and on to China.
The Sasanians took Bactria and the west in the third century and set up Kushano-Sasanian governors; the last Kushan kings ruled in the Punjab in the shadow of the Guptas until about 375.

passages.text: Later Liang was the first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel who deposed the last Tang emperor, it controlled only part of northern China and faced constant military threats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kaifeng developed as the capital, though smaller and less cosmopolitan than Tang Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Five Dynasties period saw the rise of military strongmen who dominated politics.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Printing technology continued to develop during this unstable period.
Li Cunxu of Later Tang conquered Later Liang and captured its capital Kaifeng in 923.

passages.text: The Liu Song was the first of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang. Despite political instability, this period saw significant cultural and intellectual achievements in the south.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi proposes the Daming calendar, the first in China to allow for the precession of the equinoxes.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi (429 to 500) bounds pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not bettered anywhere for about nine centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The poet Xie Lingyun (385 to 433) develops landscape poetry as a major genre.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Southern culture developed distinctive characteristics that influenced later periods.
The last Liu Song emperor was deposed by Xiao Daocheng, who founded the Southern Qi dynasty.

passages.text: Luba political life joined sacred kingship with council authority. Artworks could carry political knowledge, embody ancestral relationships, or serve highly practical purposes within elite daily life.

passages.title: Knowledge and memory
passages.text: Lukasa boards use carved forms or attached beads and shells to organize histories, genealogies and significant places. Their interpretation depends on trained specialists.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The mbudye association includes women and men who interpret political principles and can restrain or reinforce chiefly authority.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Female figures on royal seats, staffs and other court objects relate to ancestral kings and the sacred character of rule.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Carved headrests protected elaborate hairstyles while their owners slept. A nineteenth-century example repeats the hairstyle in the sculpture itself.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A headrest can create a strong sculptural composition with slender limbs and open spaces while still supporting the sleeper's head.

passages.text: Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: By 1650, Mwaant Yaav Naweej had connected his capital with Atlantic trade. This commerce included enslaved people as well as forest products.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Lunda outposts participated in copper exchange, while settlements near Lake Mweru linked the interior with eastern commercial routes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rulers commissioned artists from client peoples, including Chokwe carvers, to make prestigious court objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Accounts of Chibinda Ilunga describe a founding culture hero. They are traditions of legitimacy, not a dated eyewitness biography.

passages.title: Music and memory
passages.text: In related Chokwe court art, a chief holds a lamellophone associated with historical recitation and praise. The object shows how music and political knowledge could meet.
