passages.text: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.
The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.

passages.text: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

passages.text: Mali connected West African gold-producing regions with a wider commercial and intellectual world. Mansa Musa became internationally famous through his pilgrimage, while architecture and oral performance preserved different forms of cultural memory.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo during his pilgrimage in 1324 to 1325. His distribution of gold made a strong impression on contemporaries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque traces its initial construction to Musa's return from pilgrimage. Later rebuilding means the surviving fabric represents multiple periods.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mosque architecture and scholarship connected Timbuktu to Islamic networks while local building practices remained central.

sectionTitles: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
Growing food in a cooler environment

passages.text: East Polynesian voyagers established communities in Aotearoa around the thirteenth-century transition to the fourteenth. This early-period card follows settlement, food production and watercraft through named archaeological sites. Māori histories encompass distinct communities and traditions; this map label does not identify a single kingdom.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: At Wairau Bar, unfinished adzes and stone-working waste record the shaping of argillite brought from the Nelson and D’Urville Island region. The concentration suggests organised production, potentially supplying other communities, rather than only occasional tool repair.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Wairau Bar fishing equipment adapts Polynesian designs to local materials, including moa bone and stone where tropical pearl shell was unavailable. Middens also contain fish, shellfish, birds, dogs and marine mammals. Early livelihoods drew on several resources.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Isotope analysis distinguishes childhood environments recorded in tooth enamel from later diets recorded in bone. Wairau Bar ancestors show differences in food and likely mobility; those signals do not identify a precise birthplace for every person or a uniform diet for the settlement.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Ornaments and equipment accompanied some Wairau Bar burials, including drilled moa eggs, worked teeth and adzes. These objects document distinctive treatment of the dead. They cannot, by themselves, establish a complete hierarchy of occupations or rank among the living.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: At Triangle Flat in Golden Bay/Mohua, planting pits dated to 1290 to 1385 contained microscopic starch interpreted as kūmara-like, alongside evidence attributed to taro and yam. The finding places horticultural experimentation within the early settlement period.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: Triangle Flat lies within the customary jurisdiction of Manawhenua ki Mohua. Its garden evidence challenges the assumption that early southern settlers relied almost entirely on hunting and gathering after abandoning tropical crops. That conclusion concerns this investigated landscape, not every settlement.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A surviving canoe hull from Anaweka on the South Island’s northwest coast was shaped from native mataī wood. Internal ribs and a longitudinal stringer were carved into the hull, while lashing holes joined components. These features reveal construction knowledge beyond simply hollowing a log.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: Additional holes beside damaged lashings show repairs to the Anaweka hull. Caulking helps date its final use to approximately 1400; older wood dates do not establish when the canoe was built. Researchers reconstruct the wider vessel from a surviving component.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A turtle carved in relief on the Anaweka hull resembles motifs in other Polynesian traditions. The researchers interpret it as evidence of cultural connections. It does not establish a uniquely identifiable departure island or the biography of the people aboard.

passages.title: Communities across generations
passages.text: Local groups maintained their own authority and relationships through genealogy, mana and tapu. Exchange carried valued materials such as pounamu, obsidian and harakeke among communities. Shared practices coexisted with regional histories and changing social ties.

The map’s 1530 endpoint is a change in coverage, not the disappearance of Māori. Colonial confiscations later dispossessed many communities, while iwi, hapū and whānau continued. The kōhanga reo movement, beginning in 1982, is one example of community-led language transmission across generations.

sectionTitles: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
Carving, memory and a documented removal

passages.text: Māori communities maintained distinct iwi and hapū histories through trade, technological change and colonisation. This card follows named examples of food production, fishing, carving and language education. The imported interval ending in 1914 does not mark an end to Māori society.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: A study of seven ancestors from Tamahere site S14/487, dated about 1700 to 1780, found diets predominantly based on plants. Archaeological context supports cultivated root crops as important foods. Isotopes do not identify each meal, and this small sample cannot describe all Māori diets.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: The teeth of two children in the Tamahere study preserve a changing dietary signal consistent with weaning onto plant foods within their first two to three years. This is a finding about those children, not a universal rule for childhood across iwi.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Te Papa’s pā kahawai lure OL000106/10, dated broadly to 1750 to 1850, combines a shaped and polished pāua-shell shank with a shell barb and tightly bound muka fibre. Fine notches decorate the shell. It preserves several stages of skilled manufacture in one small fishing implement.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Kākahu provided warmth and protection, while particular cloaks also expressed status and relationships. Their continued use as esteemed gifts and at funerals connects material workmanship with honour, care and ancestral memory. Everyday use and ceremonial importance should not be treated as interchangeable.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In the early 1840s, carvers led by Raharuhi Rukupo created Te Hau ki Tūranga at Orakaiapu pā, Manutuke. The whare whakairo belongs to Ngāti Kaipōhō of Rongowhakaata. Its carved ancestors and memorial purpose joined artistic work to hapū history and relationships.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In 1867 Crown troops dismantled Te Hau ki Tūranga and removed it despite objections. Rukupo recorded that he had refused requests to give it up. This documented removal is part of the building’s history alongside its artistry.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: The Rongowhakaata settlement deed signed in 2011 acknowledges the wrongful taking of Te Hau ki Tūranga and records the Crown’s apology. The account recognises the harm caused by separating the taonga from its community.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Treaty signed in 1840 survives in texts with different meanings. The Māori text speaks of kāwanatanga in Article 1 and guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga in Article 2; the English text uses sovereignty. Treating these as identical obscures the historical disagreement.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863 enabled land confiscation from communities labelled rebellious. Confiscation also took land from Māori who had remained neutral or supported the government. The effects differed by region, with severe losses in Waikato and Taranaki.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki connects seasonal knowledge with remembrance and sharing the harvest. Communities observe it in different ways and at different times. Its significance joins practical attention to the year with relationships among the living and the dead.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Pukeatua kōhanga reo opened in Wainuiomata in April 1982. The movement places children in Māori-language immersion environments and gives whānau responsibility for running centres. Education here includes language, relationships and cultural knowledge transmitted through daily life.

Māori have no cultural fall date. Colonial war and confiscation transformed landholding and political authority, while communities persisted. Te Tiriti remains central to the history of their relationship with the Crown. Kōhanga reo exemplifies continuing whānau-led work to pass language and knowledge to future generations.

sectionTitles: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
Gardening and the work of clothing

passages.text: This record follows Māori communities in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Gardens, crafts and ancestral taonga reveal knowledge rooted in particular places. Iwi and hapū had distinct histories and authority, not a single state.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Ōtuataua Stonefields at Ihumātao preserve rows, heaps and mounds associated with cultivation on volcanic ground. The specialised system may have developed by the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Adding sand and gravel and arranging stone helped growers manage soil and growing conditions.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Shell middens at Ōtuataua, including deposits dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, show that coastal foods accompanied gardening. Habitation areas and storage features place food production within a lived landscape rather than an isolated agricultural installation.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Today’s stonefields contain features from different periods. Māori gardens, house sites, cooking shelters and terraces share the landscape with nineteenth-century European drystone walls. A visible wall is therefore not automatically evidence of a pre-contact Māori garden boundary.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: In the middle Waikato Basin, modified soils and borrow pits record intensive horticulture from the sixteenth century. Gardeners moved gravel into cultivation areas. Storage pits and planting features add evidence of sustained labour in managing root crops.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Whatu forms cloth by twining horizontal threads around vertical ones with the fingers. Muka fibre extracted from harakeke supplied material for cloaks. Raranga uses plaiting, commonly for mats and baskets. These related crafts solve different structural problems.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Rain capes combine a worked foundation with overlapping plant strips that shed water. Scraped sections allowed the strips to be attached as the garment grew. The construction joined knowledge of fibre preparation, fastening and weather protection; no exact invention date is established here.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Te Papa presents weaving’s whakapapa through Hine-te-iwaiwa, guardian of weaving, childbirth and lunar cycles. In this tradition, women transmit the skills and knowledge. Craft is understood through relationships among people, ancestors and the natural world as well as through technique.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Uenuku, an ancestral carving held at Te Awamutu Museum, represents an atua of Tainui. Tainui tradition associates the spirit of Uenuku with the voyaging waka. The museum gives a broad traditional dating range; this card does not convert it into a precise manufacture year.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki’s return to the winter dawn sky marks a new year. Remembrance, harvest thanksgiving and sharing food connect observation of the heavens with community life. Timing and observance vary among iwi; there was no single uniform national calendar.

Māori communities continue beyond this map interval. Ōtuataua retains local ancestral connections. Later colonial confiscation caused dispossession, while iwi and hapū persisted. Kōhanga reo supports continuing cultural transmission.

passages.text: The Maratha state founded by Shivaji in the Western Ghats broke Mughal power in the eighteenth century and, as a confederacy of chiefs under the Peshwa at Pune, ruled or taxed most of India by the 1750s. Its horsemen, hill forts and revenue administration made it the last great Indian power before the British.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Light cavalry that lived off the country and struck and withdrew defeated slower Mughal armies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shivaji's chain of hill forts, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad among them, controlled the passes of the Western Ghats.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A navy under Kanhoji Angre held the Konkan coast against the Portuguese, the Siddis and the East India Company.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony asserting independent Hindu kingship.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers, ran war, revenue, foreign affairs and religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Marathi, with Sanskrit terms replacing Persian ones in Shivaji's chancery, became the language of state.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Revenue came as chauth and sardeshmukhi, a quarter and a tenth of the yield, collected directly from the land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Maratha wars drained the Mughals; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the confederacy recovered and held Delhi's emperor as a client.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Marathi identity and the memory of Shivaji remain central in Maharashtra.
The East India Company beat the confederacy in three wars; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and his lands were annexed.

passages.text: Maya history encompasses distinct societies and city-states. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan supported royal courts with specialized artists; their political histories should be explored individually rather than compressed into one Maya empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Some court artists signed their work. The sculptor Chakalte' left his name on a relief showing Shield Jaguar IV receiving tribute.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved and polished limestone vessels with tools and abrasives. Shell, bone, jade and fired clay offered other media for intricate objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Blue-green jade evoked water, new growth and primordial beings. It became material for offerings, ornaments and royal regalia.

passages.title: Writing and history
passages.text: Tikal's carved and painted inscriptions preserve dynastic history and relationships with other cities. They document particular courts, not a single pan-Maya government.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Tikal combined monumental precincts with residential districts and reservoirs known today as aguadas. Its surrounding settlements also supported agricultural production.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: After several Classic-period kingdoms declined, northern centers such as Chichen Itza continued commissioning major artworks. Political collapse in one region did not end Maya history everywhere.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Tikal's Corriental reservoir, researchers identified zeolite and coarse quartz in dated sediment layers. They interpret these minerals as evidence of a water filter; its proposed stone supports and woven matting are a reconstruction, not a surviving intact installation.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Water-jar fragments occur throughout Corriental's excavated sediment sequence, linking the reservoir to everyday water collection. The filter evidence comes from this particular reservoir, not from every Maya city.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Copan, exposed layers of the Acropolis preserve earlier plaza floors and covered water outlets beneath later construction. These buried surfaces reveal repeated rebuilding of the city rather than a monument created in a single episode.

Maya societies did not share one fall date or one conqueror. UNESCO places Copan's abandonment in the early tenth century, while northern centers continued major artistic production after many Classic courts declined; a local city's decline cannot stand for the end of all Maya societies. Maya communities continue today, with living languages and cultural traditions.

passages.text: Mercia was a kingdom in central England. Large earthworks and the Staffordshire Hoard offer different views of its region: organized construction and highly skilled early medieval metalwork.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Offa's Dyke used a bank and ditch to mark a frontier. English Heritage dates its construction probably to the 780s.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Staffordshire Hoard fragments include intricate gold and garnet decoration. Their designs have connections across several European regions.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Many hoard fragments belonged to an elaborate helmet. Modern reconstruction relies on study of the surviving pieces rather than discovery of an intact helmet.

passages.title: Evidence and daily life
passages.text: The hoard reveals elite craftsmanship and equipment. Its burial location alone cannot identify every maker or make it a representative sample of ordinary Mercian households.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Scholars from Mercia contributed to the translations supported by Alfred of Wessex. Learned activity crossed the boundaries between neighboring kingdoms.

passages.text: The Marinids made Fez a royal capital and sponsored an urban culture of learning, worship, commerce and craftsmanship. Their new town stood beside the older medina, creating a capital with complementary royal and civic spaces.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Fez Jedid was founded in 1276 beside Fez el-Bali. It included the palace, fortifications, military headquarters and residential districts.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Madrasas and mosques are among the principal monuments associated with the city's Marinid flourishing in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

passages.title: Daily life and trade
passages.text: Fondouks, houses and fountains belonged to the capital's urban fabric alongside royal and religious buildings.

passages.title: Arts and legacy
passages.text: Fez's architecture brought local skills into conversation with influences from Andalusia and other African and eastern centers. Its craft traditions continued beyond any one dynasty.

passages.text: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.

passages.text: Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Potters used molds to produce standardized vessel shapes while varying their painted and sculpted decoration.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Many vessels combine red and cream slip painting with modeled figures. Complex scenes could cover the surface of a stirrup-spout bottle.

passages.title: Portraiture
passages.text: Portrait bottles may depict recognizable individuals. Scholars debate how their social identities related to the vessels' eventual placement in burials.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Fine decorated pottery also occurs in residential compounds. Wear, repairs and excavated household contexts show that many vessels served the living before burial.

passages.title: Food and gatherings
passages.text: Decorated vessels participated in household rituals and feasts, including the sharing of food and corn beer.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Images include crops, animals, healers and supernatural beings. They are a visual source, but an image alone cannot tell us every detail of the activity it depicts.

passages.text: Mossi political history includes several kingdoms in present-day Burkina Faso. Their populations developed through conquest, migration and incorporation of existing communities. Ouagadougou was influential, but it was not an ancient capital governing every Mossi kingdom.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Duperray’s research describes kingdoms formed through encounters between incoming ruling lineages and established populations. Political incorporation did not erase differences of origin. This helps explain why a single map label covers multiple communities and centres of authority.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Yarse communities included Muslim merchants. Oral traditions link many lineages with Mande origins, while others became Yarse through local relationships. Duperray’s interviews reveal changing identities rather than a merchant population with one uniform ancestry.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: The protectorate treaty of January 1897 helped France claim a wider territory. Beucher argues that officials enlarged the apparent authority of Ouagadougou’s ruler, the Moogo Naaba, to justify colonial control. The resulting hierarchy cannot simply be projected backward.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A Smithsonian Mossi vessel, made in the middle or late twentieth century, carries impressed patterns below and incised zigzags above. The museum describes pottery used for water, grain, cooking and brewing beer, placing decorated ceramics within ordinary household work.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The Smithsonian’s technique account describes shaping clay over a mould, then adding coils to build the upper vessel. Drying, decoration and firing followed. Millet stalks, wood and manure supplied fuel. Both men and women participated in these pottery traditions.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A late twentieth-century Mossi shawl in the British Museum consists of thirteen narrow cotton strips sewn together. Handspun thread, indigo dye and additional patterned weft at the ends show several kinds of work within one textile.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The museum suggests this cloth may be a diisa prestige shawl, given by a mother to a son on marriage and later used as a burial shroud. That social interpretation is qualified; it is not a securely documented biography of this particular textile.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The High Museum’s karan-wemba figure represents an honoured older woman. Its ridged coiffure and geometric bodily marks connect sculpture with appearance and social status. Patt relates the work to Yatenga traditions while stressing differences among Mossi artistic communities.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: Radiocarbon analysis placed the High Museum figure’s wood around the sixteenth century. Wood age does not establish when an artist carved it. Patt considers the possibility of a much later sculpture made from old timber, so an exact early creation date remains unproven.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The PLU collection account describes carving masks from green wood with an adze and knife, then smoothing them with rough leaves. A mask’s performance required further work: fibre fittings, clothing and rattles connected the carved object with a moving, sounding costume.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The same account places cooking, grinding and grain storage within household compounds. These workspaces connect the material arts with food preparation and farming. They describe recorded Mossi settings, not a single house plan shared by every kingdom or historical century.

French forces occupied Ouagadougou in September 1896, followed by the 1897 protectorate. Other kingdoms had their own encounters with colonial rule. Royal authority was constrained and reshaped; this political change did not mark the disappearance of Mossi people or their artistic traditions.

passages.text: Muscogee histories connect southeastern ancestral places, a changing network of towns and continuing nations. Ocmulgee's surviving clay architecture, town councils and later government buildings show different forms of collective life. The later Creek Confederacy and the present Muscogee Nation must not be projected unchanged onto the map's fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Ocmulgee is an ancestral homeland of the Muscogee Nation. Its long occupation is evidence of successive communities at a place; it does not establish that the later Creek Confederacy existed throughout all those earlier centuries.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The Earth Lodge preserves an original clay floor dating approximately to the early eleventh century. The enclosing walls and roof visitors see were reconstructed in the 1930s. Separating those elements helps distinguish surviving archaeology from a modern interpretation of the building.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Seats, a central hearth and a raised bird effigy were formed into the floor. Their arrangement supports interpretation as a special gathering place. Differences in seating do not by themselves establish a complete social hierarchy, an interpretation the park's bulletin explicitly questions.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The round lodge used internal roof supports, while nearby houses were usually smaller and rectangular. Different building forms reveal deliberate choices about public and domestic space. The exact meanings of the bird's imagery remain uncertain.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Historic towns placed council houses beside ceremonial plazas, with grounds for ball play and chunkey nearby. A meko worked with advisers. These spaces joined public decisions, gatherings and recreation within a town.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Maternal clans organized belonging, while people also maintained ties to particular towns. The confederacy included speakers of different languages. A shared political network did not erase those local relationships and differences.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: During the eighteenth century, deerskin commerce displaced the earlier trade in enslaved people. Relations with colonial traders affected town alliances and livelihoods. Exchange offered opportunities while also drawing communities into violent external demands.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Before removal, Muscogee households included farmers and cattle owners, and some people enslaved others. This varied economy matters: forced migration uprooted established livelihoods and also carried the coercion of slavery into the new western setting.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: From 1878 to Oklahoma statehood in 1907, the Council House at Okmulgee housed the Principal Chief, Supreme Court, education offices and National Council chambers. Its rooms show government as everyday administrative work as well as public ceremony.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The Nation was forced to leave the building at statehood and regained it in 2010. Restoration completed in 2018 recovered its historic room layout for interpretation. Regaining a building was an act of stewardship by an existing Nation, not the creation of a new people.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The constitution's election certificate records ratification on 6 October 1979. Its separate executive, legislative and judicial articles set out national institutions, while article II protects the organization of tribal towns. The document records both change and continuing local traditions.

passages.title: Removal and survival
passages.text: In 1836 and 1837, United States authorities forced large numbers of Muscogee people toward Indian Territory by land and water. Detention, inadequate supplies and dangerous travel caused profound suffering. Communities rebuilt afterward while maintaining ties to southeastern homelands.

Coerced land cessions and removal transformed Muscogee political geography in the nineteenth century. Later allotment and statehood imposed further losses, but the Muscogee Nation and its communities continue. The map's 1492 to 1500 interval is not a supported lifespan for the people or the later confederacy.

passages.text: The Nara period gave Japan its first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo, laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. The court ran the country under the ritsuryo codes, made Buddhism a state religion and compiled its first histories and poetry.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Manyoshu, an anthology of 4,516 poems by emperors, courtiers and frontier guards, was compiled; its latest dated poem is from 759.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Kojiki, and in 720 the Nihon Shoki, recorded the myths and early history of the imperial line.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze figure about 15 meters high, was dedicated in a ceremony attended by monks from India and China.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Shomu ordered a state temple and nunnery in every province.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ritsuryo codes, the Taiho of 701 and the Yoro of 718, organized government, taxes and land on Tang models.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning was taught at the state academy to train officials.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese characters were used for all government records, and census and tax registers were kept on paper.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Trunk roads with post stations linked the capital to the provinces.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Manyoshu remains the foundation of Japanese poetry.
Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, in 794, the start of the Heian period.

sectionTitles: Conquest and lives beyond the court

passages.text: Ndongo was a kingdom in the Kimbundu-speaking region of present-day Angola. Its ruler, the Ngola, held authority through relationships with local polities. Its political history cannot be reduced to a fixed territory ruled uniformly from one capital.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: The Kwanza corridor connected farming, pastoralism, iron production and salt supplies with trading settlements. Angola’s heritage account places this exchange before Portuguese conquest. Food and working materials circulated alongside the later expansion of captive trading.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: Kabasa, also written Cabaça, was both a royal centre and an important market. Other fairs operated under royal officers. Markets supplied neighbouring communities and linked more distant places, making their regulation a practical part of government.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: River navigation linked parts of the interior with coastal exchange. The Kwanza had both navigable stretches and obstacles; overland paths and scattered markets also mattered. The trading landscape was a network of different routes, not one uninterrupted river highway.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Local sobas governed smaller polities that entered the king’s orbit through conquest or agreement. Thornton describes expansion as incorporation of these units. Their own rulers remained important, helping explain why alliances could shift during wars with the Portuguese.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Jesuit accounts from the 1580s recorded hundreds of local political units. Thornton treats the unusually precise reported count as possible evidence of fiscal knowledge gained at court. It is testimony about administration, not a modern census independently confirmed for every settlement.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Kijiko were unfree people who could hold revenue-collecting roles. Capturing them disrupted Ndongo’s administration. Fonseca stresses that Portuguese translations as “slaves” can conceal these particular functions.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: At Kindonga, Njinga’s supporters stored food and weapons on Kwanza islands. Their knowledge of branching channels helped them avoid pursuing forces. Geography, provisioning and local experience worked together in resistance.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: A lunga, a double metal bell, marked authority in a military camp. Fonseca describes a demand that Njinga surrender hers when seeking an ally’s protection, linking a tangible object with a political negotiation.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Njinga offered refuge to people escaping enslavement and recruited African soldiers trained in Portuguese service. This brought people with different experiences into her following. Protection and military organisation helped rebuild power after displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Resistance to Portuguese conquest did not mean opposition to all enslavement. From Matamba, Njinga exchanged captives for Dutch support and firearms. Her alliances could protect followers while harming those captured as enemies.

passages.title: Conquest and lives beyond the court
passages.text: After Pungo Andongo fell in 1671, members of the royal family were deported to Brazil and later Portugal. Lara follows these exiles through Atlantic records. The kingdom’s defeat continued in the displacement of identifiable people, beyond the battlefield itself.

Portuguese forces captured Pungo Andongo in 1671 after a siege, killing its ruler and ending that royal centre’s resistance. Njinga had died in Matamba in 1663. These separate events should not be collapsed into one ruler’s defeat or the disappearance of Mbundu communities.

passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Dutch engineers and designers experimented with ways to manage water and domestic space. This chapter pairs a steam pumping station with an adaptable family home.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda pumping station opened at Lemmer in 1920 to help prevent flooding in low-lying Friesland, using steam power to move water.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda installation integrated a boiler house, chimney, fuel storage, drainage canal and sluices. Water management required an entire connected system.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Truus Schroder-Schrader commissioned the house designed by Gerrit Rietveld in Utrecht in 1924. Its design expressed ideas associated with De Stijl.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Schroder House used a flexible internal arrangement so rooms could change with their functions. Furniture and interior space were treated as parts of one design.

passages.text: Aotearoa New Zealand's history includes Māori settlement and innovation, colonization, campaigns for rights and the development of a modern state. Archaeological remains, carved buildings, petitions and homes reveal both achievement and unequal power. Constitutional independence developed through several steps; no single change of title explains the whole story.

passages.title: Early settlement seen through archaeology
passages.text: Research places Polynesian settlement of Aotearoa around 1300 CE. At Wairau Bar, evidence extends beyond burials to structures, cooking and stone-tool production. A large stone-lined oven and animal remains help reconstruct village activities during an early phase of Māori history.

passages.title: Early settlement seen through archaeology
passages.text: The 2009 Wairau Bar research followed an invitation from Rangitāne mana whenua alongside the return and reburial of ancestral remains. Geophysical survey and excavation examined the wider settlement. The history of research therefore includes community authority and relationships, as well as what was found.

passages.title: Carving, architecture and colonial loss
passages.text: Raharuhi Rukupō began Te Hau-ki-Tūranga at Manutūkē in 1842 as a memorial to his elder brother. Expert carvers worked on its posts and structure. Rukupō learned inherited techniques and later adopted steel tools, showing innovation within an established artistic tradition.

passages.title: Carving, architecture and colonial loss
passages.text: The government had Te Hau-ki-Tūranga dismantled and removed in 1867 during the confiscation of Tūranga lands. Payments went to people later found not to be its owners. Its subsequent museum display must therefore be understood alongside the coercive circumstances of removal.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its English counterpart were signed in 1840, but their terms concerning authority differ. The Māori text uses kāwanatanga and guarantees tino rangatiratanga; the English text speaks of sovereignty. Those differences matter when interpreting what rangatira and the Crown understood they had agreed.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: The surviving 1893 women's suffrage petition consists of sheets gathered across the country and pasted into a roll by Kate Sheppard. Its physical form records collective organizing through meetings, travel and persuasion, not only the actions of a single prominent campaigner.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: The Electoral Act signed on 19 September 1893 gave women the parliamentary vote. Earlier petition campaigns had failed in the Legislative Council. The successful reform followed repeated organizing and political struggle rather than a sudden, unopposed concession.

passages.title: Technology, food and work
passages.text: The sailing ship Dunedin carried a successful frozen-meat shipment to Britain in 1882 using a coal-powered freezing plant. Meat from Totara Estate moved by rail to Port Chalmers before freezing aboard. The achievement depended on an organized chain of workers, transport and temperature control.

passages.title: Technology, food and work
passages.text: Refrigerated shipping needed marketing and insurance arrangements as well as machinery. Its growth supported meat and dairy exports and reshaped farming. This was an application and organization of refrigeration technology, not evidence that refrigeration itself was invented in New Zealand.

passages.title: Homes and ordinary lives
passages.text: The house at 12 Fife Lane in Miramar opened in 1937 as the first of the Labour government's new state houses. Photographs of the opening made it a public symbol, but for David and Mary McGregor it was also a family home entered by crowds of visitors.

passages.title: Homes and ordinary lives
passages.text: David McGregor worked as a tram driver. The family initially paid rent and later bought the house under a changed policy. Following one household links a national housing program with wages, tenure and the practical wish for a secure place to live.

passages.title: Scientific work across borders
passages.text: Born and educated in New Zealand, Ernest Rutherford developed the nuclear model of the atom in 1911 while working in Manchester. Scattering experiments involving Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden helped establish a small central nucleus. His achievement belongs to an international research setting, not an isolated national invention.

passages.title: Changing constitutional relationships
passages.text: New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster on 25 November 1947. The Constitution Act 1986 later removed the remaining provision for British legislation. These milestones show a gradual change in the state's relationship with Britain, rather than an independence date inferred from a map boundary.

New Zealand continues as a state. Its relationship with Britain changed through dominion status, the 1947 statute adoption and later constitutional reform. Māori communities and authority have their own continuing histories, including the unresolved consequences of colonial land loss and differing understandings of Te Tiriti.

sectionTitles: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers

passages.text: Ngarrindjeri communities connect the lower Murray, lakes, Coorong and Sea Country through law, kinship, food and cultural responsibility. Fishing technology, feather flowers and David Unaipon's papers reveal skill and invention in different settings. Their history continues through dispossession, environmental disruption, community teaching and public advocacy.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: The community's Sea Country Plan describes Tendi as a council that makes and interprets Ngarrindjeri law. Ngartji relationships with particular animals and plants bring obligations to care for them and their habitats.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: Fish, shellfish, waterbirds and plants supported settled life and gatherings. Nets made from bulrush fibers, bone or shell hooks, stone traps and woven weirs show different ways of working with water and animal behavior.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: Bark canoes, reed rafts and floating platforms supported work on the water. Food storage and smoke-drying fish helped supply gatherings and exchange with neighboring communities. These practices joined making, preservation and social relationships.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: A bouquet made at Point McLeay in the 1920s, now in the National Museum of Australia, uses feathers from pelicans and other Coorong birds. Makers drew dye from crepe paper soaked in water, then colored the feathers. The object records skilled adaptation of available materials.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: The Point McLeay mission began in 1859 on land too small for the families moved there. Ngarrindjeri people developed fishing, boat making, wool washing, weaving and other enterprises. Feather flowers provided income while also carrying ecological and artistic knowledge.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: Changes to river flows and wetlands affect materials as well as food. The museum account describes freshwater sedges used in weaving becoming scarcer. Maintaining a craft therefore also depends on the health and accessibility of the places that supply it.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: Patent 15624, dated 3 September 1909, records David Unaipon's improved mechanical motion device. Applied to sheep shearing, it converted rotary movement into straight-line motion. The patent and accompanying diagrams provide a specific record of an inventor working on an industrial problem.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: In an April 1914 letter to Herbert Basedow, Unaipon asked for financial help to develop his machine. A following memorandum offered conditional government assistance. These papers reveal the difficulty of obtaining support; a patent alone does not demonstrate profitable manufacture.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: Unaipon also collected and wrote stories. Material from his manuscript appeared under William Ramsay Smith's name in 1930. Work with Unaipon's descendants later restored his authorship in the 2001 publication of Legendary Tales of the Australian Aborigines.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: Elder Ellen Trevorrow teaches weaving and cultural storytelling at Camp Coorong. Her work connects the making of baskets and sculpture with learning across generations. Participants learn through shared activity and conversation as well as looking at finished objects.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: Camp Coorong activities also include walks with Elders to learn about animals, food plants and Country. Such teaching connects practical knowledge with the responsibility to understand and care for the places where it is used.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: The Sea Country Plan describes colonial land loss and mission pressure on language and belief. Its response is continuing Ngarrindjeri participation in decisions about land and waters, with cultural responsibilities informing future management.

Ngarrindjeri people and cultural life continue. Dispossession and changes to rivers and wetlands damaged livelihoods and access to Country, but Raukkan, Camp Coorong and living artistic practices show continuing community history. There is no single fall year or successor state that describes that experience.

sectionTitles: Cloth in daily use and burial

passages.text: Nobatia, also called Nobadia, was a kingdom of Lower Nubia. Houses, royal burials and churches reveal different settings of life. Its later union with Makuria changed political institutions while regional communities and crafts continued.

passages.title: Houses and food storage
passages.text: Early Nobatian houses at Qasr Ibrim had substantial stone walls, internal divisions and storage pits beneath floors. Straight intersecting lanes organised the settlement. The pits preserve evidence of keeping provisions within buildings.

passages.title: Houses and food storage
passages.text: Later houses at Qasr Ibrim used smaller stones, mud-brick partitions and compacted-earth floors. Some retained sunken storage bins. Building techniques changed while household storage continued.

passages.title: Royal display and its limits
passages.text: The great burial mounds at Qustul and Ballana cover elaborate underground tombs. Rich objects and the remains of sacrificed animals and people accompanied elite burials. They reveal concentrated power and coercion, rather than the living conditions of an average family.

passages.title: Royal display and its limits
passages.text: Greek texts identify the kingdom as Noubadia and name Silko among its rulers. This written evidence helps connect political names with an archaeological landscape. The older label “X-Group” describes a research classification, not the people’s own name.

passages.title: Cloth in daily use and burial
passages.text: At Qasr Ibrim, seams and hems allow researchers to distinguish some garments from otherwise unidentifiable scraps. Early medieval cotton also survives in cushions and reused rags used as mattress filling. Cloth could pass through several uses before entering the archaeological record.

passages.title: Cloth in daily use and burial
passages.text: Early Christian graves at Kulubnarti contain unusually open cotton fabrics interpreted as shrouds. Other funerary bindings combine light plant fibres with dark wool. These finds show choices in fibre, structure and colour, but burial cloth cannot stand for an entire everyday wardrobe.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: The early seventh-century church at Faras was followed by a later cathedral. Surviving wall paintings were applied in tempera to plaster. Most of the preserved paintings date from the eighth to fourteenth centuries, after independent Nobatia.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: Faras preserves epitaphs naming clergy and locally produced pottery alongside its painted walls. These are different kinds of evidence for a religious community: written remembrance, workshop production and decorated spaces used for worship.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: In later medieval Nubia, painters of luxury pottery adapted motifs also found in manuscripts and church decoration. Some broken bowls were drilled and stitched together again. These repairs reveal the value attached to decorated vessels and the work invested in extending their use.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: Medieval Nubian texts survive in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, sometimes combining languages. Religious fragments and commercial or legal documents preserve different uses of writing. This later record should not be projected unchanged into the earlier independent kingdom.

Nobatia joined Makuria, but the timing remains debated. Obłuski discusses proposed seventh-century dates and evidence associating unification with King Merkurios around the early eighth century. Regional communities continued under changed institutions; Faras’s later cathedral paintings make that continuity tangible. The imported map endpoint is not a verified conquest date.

passages.text: The Northern Wei was founded by the Tuoba clan of the Xianbei people and became the most successful of the Northern Dynasties. It promoted Buddhism, sinicization policies and created institutions that influenced later Chinese dynasties.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Yungang cave temples carved near Datong, with massive Buddha statues.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Xiaowen moves the capital to Luoyang and orders the Xianbei to adopt Chinese language, dress and surnames; work on the Longmen caves begins the year before.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The equal-field system implemented, distributing land to peasant households.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The equal-field system became a model for Sui and Tang land policies.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Buddhist cave temples at Yungang and Longmen remain major artistic achievements.
Internal conflicts between military factions split Northern Wei into Eastern Wei in 534 and Western Wei in 535.

passages.text: Northumbria joined the regions of Bernicia and Deira. Its royal centers and monasteries supported learning, manuscript production and religious networks reaching beyond northern Britain.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: King Oswald invited Aidan from Iona to establish a monastery at Lindisfarne in 635. Royal support placed the foundation near the kingdom's political center.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Lindisfarne Gospels were made approximately 710 to 725. They are evidence of the monastery's role as a center of Christian learning and book production.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Pilgrims came to Cuthbert's shrine, while patrons gave land, money and precious objects. Religious devotion helped support the monastery's economy.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Runic name stones commemorate Anglo-Saxon inhabitants of Lindisfarne, preserving writing outside the pages of books.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: The monastic community moved inland during Viking-era disruption, carrying treasures and relics. Carved stones show that Christian burial continued on Lindisfarne after the monks left.

passages.text: Medieval Norway developed through a long process of political consolidation, rather than a single securely dated founding. Timber churches, waterfront buildings, inscribed sticks and legal manuscripts show how people built, traded and communicated. Later royal unions changed the kingdom's independence; they did not end Norwegian communities or their accumulated knowledge.

passages.title: Timber engineering and reused art
passages.text: Urnes Stave Church translates a basilica layout into timber. Columns, arches, roof framing and shingles worked together to create a substantial interior. The building shows carpenters adapting an architectural language familiar from stone churches to a different material.

passages.title: Timber engineering and reused art
passages.text: Urnes reuses carved elements from an eleventh-century predecessor, including interlaced animals on the north wall. Older craft remained visible within a later Christian building. Reuse means the date of a carving and the date of its present setting can differ.

passages.title: Timber engineering and reused art
passages.text: The surviving church rests on a sill frame above stone foundations, unlike an earlier structure with posts set into the ground. Medieval furnishings and later alterations also survive. The site records successive solutions to building and worship, rather than one unchanging moment.

passages.title: Food, storage and waterfront work
passages.text: Bergen connected northern Norwegian stockfish producers with wider markets. Hanseatic merchants gained royal trading privileges and developed a permanent presence at Bryggen. The trade joined fishing and preservation to transport, storage and negotiation over access to markets.

passages.title: Food, storage and waterfront work
passages.text: Bryggen's narrow plots placed homes and offices near the harbour, warehouses farther back, and communal rooms and kitchens behind them. Stone storerooms protected valuable goods from fire. This arrangement made the waterfront both a workplace and a setting for communal living.

passages.title: Food, storage and waterfront work
passages.text: Repeated fires destroyed Bryggen's buildings, which were rebuilt on earlier plots using traditional techniques. Much of today's appearance follows the fire of 1702. A medieval plan can survive through replacement buildings, so the standing timber should not all be dated to the Middle Ages.

passages.title: Messages and legal learning
passages.text: A thirteenth-century tally stick from Bugarden at Bryggen carries counting notches on one side and an affectionate runic message on another. Catalogued as B118, it brings commercial record-keeping and personal communication together on a small wooden object.

passages.title: Messages and legal learning
passages.text: Another Bugarden stick, dated to the middle decades of the thirteenth century, combines an affectionate request with the opening letters of the runic alphabet. The alphabet could have carried magical meaning, but its precise use remains an interpretation, not a directly observed ritual.

passages.title: Messages and legal learning
passages.text: Magnus VI introduced the National Law in 1274, bringing regional assembly traditions into a kingdom-wide legal framework. Surviving handwritten copies preserve the work of scribes as well as legislators. A separate City Law followed in 1276, reflecting distinct needs of urban communities.

passages.title: Messages and legal learning
passages.text: Copies of the National Law disagree over retaliation and other sensitive rules, including poor relief and women's rights. Those variations make the manuscripts evidence of contested legal change. The text of a royal law does not demonstrate that every court or household followed it uniformly.

passages.title: Institutions through changing rule
passages.text: Erik's coronation at Kalmar in 1397 brought Norway, Denmark and Sweden under a shared monarch. Historians still debate parts of the agreement's legal meaning. Sharing a king was not initially the same as abolishing each realm's council and separate political identity.

passages.title: Institutions through changing rule
passages.text: The Reformation imposed in 1536 and 1537 replaced medieval church arrangements with Lutheran institutions under the king. The Church of Norway's history distinguishes that official change from its slower reception among ordinary people. Government decisions and lived religious practice followed different timelines.

Royal military intervention in 1537, following Christian III's commitments in 1536, sharply reduced Norway's autonomy and ended its medieval council and Catholic church province. Norway remained a recognisable kingdom within a Danish-centred monarchy, with continuing communities and local administration. The map endpoint of 1400 does not mark this transition or a cultural extinction.

passages.text: Numidian society belongs to North Africa's indigenous history and its wider Mediterranean connections. Thugga, now Dougga, offers evidence for urban life under Numidian kings and for its transformation under Roman rule. The spectacular Roman monuments there are later additions to an older town.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: At Thugga, Roman construction was fitted into a largely Numidian street pattern. Urban continuity survived the change of political authority.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Libyan, Punic and bilingual inscriptions help reconstruct Numidian social and municipal life. Their study also contributed to deciphering Libyan writing.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Libyco-Punic mausoleum preserves an important pre-Roman monumental tradition, although its modern reconstruction complicates interpretation of the standing structure.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Under Rome, an indigenous community and a legally distinct group of Roman citizens coexisted at Thugga. Cultural change did not require the town's earlier inhabitants to vanish.

passages.text: Olmec names a group of early Mesoamerican societies, especially those of Mexico's Gulf Coast. Their monumental building projects and stoneworking joined local farming communities to far-reaching networks of materials and artistic ideas.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At San Lorenzo, communities cooperated to build large earthen platforms and mounds. These were shared construction projects beyond the needs of individual households.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Artists worked both enormous volcanic-stone sculptures and small, finely finished jade objects. Those materials could travel from distant sources.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maize farming helped sustain communities in Gulf Coast river valleys, although many details of San Lorenzo's households remain under investigation.

passages.title: Games
passages.text: Rubber balls recovered at El Manati provide early evidence for the place of ballgames in Olmec life.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: La Venta's carvings connect rulers with watery environments and agricultural fertility. Their imagery draws on the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: La Venta flourished especially between 1000 and 500 BCE and was apparently abandoned by 400 BCE. That local sequence does not establish one universal fall for all Olmec societies.

passages.text: The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Theodoric's mausoleum used large blocks of Istrian stone arranged around a central space.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo began as Theodoric's palace chapel. Its mosaics combined Roman traditions with eastern Mediterranean influence.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arian Baptistery preserves imagery expressing the court's Christian faith. The Archbishop's Chapel represents a different Christian community in the same city.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: In wider Ostrogothic dress, pairs of shoulder brooches secured women's long garments. Decorated belts, necklaces and other jewelry completed the ensemble.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A surviving brooch attributed to wider Ostrogothic material culture was cast in silver, with silver covering its copper-alloy pin. It combined practical fastening and ornament; the record does not establish manufacture in Italy.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Ravenna passed from Ostrogothic to Byzantine rule. Buildings surviving together today belong to different patrons and periods; San Vitale's Justinianic decoration should not be credited to Theodoric.

passages.text: The kingdom of Pagan, on the Irrawaddy, united the Burmese lands under Anawrahta in the 1050s and made Theravada Buddhism the faith of the country. Its kings and people covered the plain of Bagan with thousands of temples in two hundred years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: More than 2,000 temples and stupas still stand at Bagan out of some 10,000 built between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ananda temple, finished about 1105 under Kyansittha, with its four standing Buddhas and gilded spire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Burmese writing, adapted from the Mon script, appears on the Myazedi inscription of 1113 beside Pyu, Mon and Pali.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Anawrahta adopted Theravada Buddhism under the Mon monk Shin Arahan and in 1057 took Thaton, bringing its monks and scriptures to Pagan.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Contacts with Sri Lanka in the twelfth century renewed the monastic ordination and the Pali canon.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Weirs and canals in the Kyaukse district fed the rice that paid for the temples.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bagan was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism remains the religion of most of Myanmar.

Mongol armies invaded in 1277 and 1287, and King Narathihapate fled and was murdered by his own son. His successors ruled as Mongol vassals until the three brothers of Myinsaing deposed the last of them in 1297.

passages.text: The Parthian Empire, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty from 247 BCE to 224 CE, held Iran and Mesopotamia between Rome and the steppe for nearly five centuries. Its armored lancers and horse archers, its great noble houses and its grip on the Silk Road made it Rome's only equal in the East.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Parthian shot: horse archers turned in the saddle to shoot behind them at full gallop.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Carrhae in 53 BCE, horse archers and cataphracts, riders and horses in scale armor, destroyed a Roman army under Crassus.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire sat astride the Silk Road; Chinese silk reached Rome through Parthian middlemen who kept the two ends apart.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Envoys from Han China reached the Parthian court in the 110s BCE, and in 97 CE the Han envoy Gan Ying got as far as the Persian Gulf.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Babylonian and Jewish communities kept their own cults, and the kings styled themselves friends of the Greeks on their coins.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arsacids claimed descent from the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Sasanians inherited Parthian cavalry, provinces and great noble houses.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Parthian, a Middle Iranian language written in its own script, was still used in the Sasanian royal inscriptions.
Ardashir I of Persis defeated and killed the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty.

passages.text: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Their history survives in carved stones, workshops, food remains and outside accounts. The evidence reveals connected regional societies, not a single unchanged state. Political authority and language changed as Alba emerged, without a securely established single date when all Picts disappeared.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Written references to Picts begin in the late third century. This first surviving name is not a secure founding date for a people or kingdom.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Fortriu, a powerful kingdom by the seventh century, is now located around the Moray Firth. Its full extent and relationship with smaller regions remain debated.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Rhynie's fifth- and sixth-century settlement had successive ditches and a larger timber palisade. The Craw Stane stood near an entrance. These excavated relationships connect symbol stones with an inhabited, repeatedly remodelled place.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: An iron axe-shaped pin from Rhynie resembles the axe on the Rhynie Man stone. Clay moulds for comparable pins establish local manufacture, linking a carved image to the work of metalworkers.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Rhynie's ditch deposits contained imported amphora fragments, continental glass, crucibles and metalworking tools. The vessels demonstrate exchange connections, while production debris shows that the settlement also made valuable objects.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Around 700, Portmahomack's workers carved stone, worked metal and glass, and processed hides interpreted as parchment production. Combined with its burial pattern and infrastructure, this supports identification as a monastery.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Cattle bones dominate Portmahomack's animal remains. The researchers connect cattle with food, possible dairying and hides for parchment. Supporting a religious community required husbandry and skilled processing as well as prayer.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: After the monastic phase, a Portmahomack workshop became a kiln barn with an upper floor and flue. Its alteration, together with grain remains, makes a change in everyday work visible in the buildings.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Charred barley and evidence for oats and wheat at Lairg document cultivation from about 450 onward. Such environmental traces reveal food production even where early medieval houses are difficult to identify.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: The Hilton of Cadboll cross-slab, erected around 800, places a woman prominently in a hunting scene. The original was later cut and reused as a grave marker; the stone at the site today is a replica.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Bede reports that King Naiton asked Ceolfrid for guidance on Easter and builders for a stone church. His account shows royal interest in religious calculation and imported expertise, although it presents these exchanges through Bede's Christian viewpoint.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Burning and broken sculpture mark Portmahomack's destruction around 800. A Viking raid is a proposed explanation, not an identified attacker. Workers subsequently cleared debris and resumed metal and glass production.

Pictish power centres shifted during the later ninth century, and Alba extended uneven authority into the Highlands in the tenth. This was a prolonged political and cultural transformation. The evidence does not support one conquest date or the disappearance of an entire population.

sectionTitles: Learning, patronage and the wider state

passages.text: Medieval Poland developed from Piast centres into a kingdom with towns, religious communities, mining enterprises and a university. Its political geography changed through fragmentation and renewed royal authority. Bridges, excavated buildings, municipal layouts and written records offer different views of everyday work and learning. The union with Lithuania in 1569 transformed the state while the Polish Crown continued within the Commonwealth.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Remains of two tenth-century wooden bridges lie in Lake Lednica beside the island stronghold. They connected its palace and chapel complex with routes towards Poznan and Gniezno. The timbers document organised construction and access across water, beyond the history of individual rulers.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Excavators uncovered two depressions in the Lednica chapel in 1988 and 1989. The museum interprets them as baptismal basins. They support discussion of early Christian practice, but identifying them with Mieszko's own baptism remains an interpretation rather than a witnessed event.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: At Giecz, foundations of an unfinished palace and chapel belong to the late tenth century; a stone stronghold church dates to the early eleventh. Unfinished work is evidence too: a surviving plan does not mean the planned building was completed or used.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Krakow's charter of 1257 helped shape a merchants' town whose market, streets and public buildings remain legible. Wawel formed a distinct royal and episcopal centre. The city's accumulated buildings reflect repeated construction, not a single medieval building campaign.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Kazimierz, chartered in 1335, began as a separate town beside Krakow. Catholic and Jewish communities shaped its later streets, religious buildings and customs. Its medieval origin should not be used to assign every surviving synagogue or house to the founding year.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Wieliczka produced salt from brine before deep mining expanded in the thirteenth century. An exploratory shaft found in the Saltworks Castle courtyard preserves evidence of that transition. The casing shown to visitors has been reconstructed, so the presentation includes both remains and modern interpretation.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: By the late thirteenth century, the Cracow Saltworks joined mines and salt-processing facilities at Wieliczka and Bochnia. Administration and sales connected underground labour to royal income and distant markets. The enterprise needed coordination above ground as well as extraction below it.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: The mines preserve galleries, tools and spaces later adapted for chapels or storage. UNESCO cautions that much surviving technical evidence is from the eighteenth century onward. Medieval methods are partly known from documents and reconstructions; the whole visitor route is not a medieval workplace.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Casimir III founded the University of Krakow in 1364. Teaching faltered after his death, and a renewed charter followed in 1400 through the patronage of Jadwiga and Wladyslaw Jagiello. Institutional continuity required renewed resources and organisation rather than one founding act alone.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Endowed university chairs supported subjects including astronomy, mathematics, grammar and rhetoric. The Corpus Academicum project identifies patrons such as Jan Stobner and Katarzyna Mezykowa. Teaching depended on people financing particular posts, not only on royal sponsorship.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Fifteenth-century Krakow attracted scholars in law and mathematical astronomy. Nicolaus Copernicus began his studies there in 1491. His attendance belongs to the history of this teaching community; it should not imply that all his later astronomical work was completed at the university.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: The 1569 Act of the Union of Lublin records a new constitutional relationship between the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. A surviving legal act makes the transition more specific than describing Poland as simply falling to a neighbouring country.

The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth in 1569. Polish institutions and communities continued within that arrangement. The imported map interval ending in 1400 is neither the kingdom's extinction nor the date of this constitutional transformation.
